items.q: An estimated ~80% of business data is unstructured. Why does this drive interest in machine learning?
options: Because unstructured data is easy to store in an RDBMS
Because unstructured data (text, images, video) has no schema, so ML/cognitive computing are needed to extract meaning
Because ML only works on tabular data
Because structured data cannot be analyzed
items.explain: Unstructured data lacks a logical schema, so traditional query tools fail. ML and cognitive computing are the practical way to derive insight from text, speech, images, and video.

items.q: A wind-farm operator wants to estimate each turbine's remaining useful life from vibration trends. This is which analytics type?
items.explain: Forecasting future outcomes (remaining useful life) from historical/real-time data using ML/statistical models is predictive analytics. Prescriptive would then recommend the optimal maintenance action.

items.q: In a smart factory, Spark cleans noise and computes hourly summaries before ML runs. Which pipeline stage is this?
items.explain: Cleaning, normalizing, and aggregating raw data into usable form is the data-processing (transformation) stage, sitting between storage and analytics. Stream/batch tools (Spark, Kafka, Hadoop) operate here.

items.q: When should you prefer supervised over unsupervised learning for an IoT task?
options: When you have no labels and just want to explore structure
When you can define 'success' precisely, obtain labels at reasonable cost, and need measurable, SLA-grade accuracy
items.explain: Supervised learning fits when success is precisely definable, labels are obtainable, and you need measurable accuracy (e.g., false negatives <1%). Unsupervised suits unlabeled exploration (clustering, anomaly detection).

options: Uses only labeled data end to end
Uses unsupervised learning to find clusters/anomalies, partially labels the results, then trains a supervised model — combining discovery with prediction accuracy
items.explain: Hybrid/semi-supervised approaches first cluster or detect anomalies (unsupervised), label those results, then feed them to a supervised model — blending pattern discovery with prediction accuracy (e.g., labeling energy clusters then classifying).

items.q: Why are decision trees particularly favored for IoT classification despite more accurate models existing?
options: They are highly interpretable — you can read off exactly why a device was classified 'faulty'
items.explain: Decision trees are flowchart-like and transparent: each decision is explicit, so engineers can trace the exact reasoning (e.g., temperature>30 AND vibration>X → faulty) — valuable for trust and debugging in IoT.

items.q: A wearable classifies accelerometer/gyroscope data into Walking/Running/Sleeping. The leaf nodes represent:
items.explain: Leaf nodes hold the final predicted classes (Walking/Running/Sleeping). Internal nodes test features (e.g., acceleration magnitude), and branches are the outcomes leading toward a leaf.

items.q: A remote oil rig needs sub-second control decisions and must keep operating when its satellite link drops. The best architecture is:
options: Edge-based (local processing for low latency and offline resilience), syncing to the cloud periodically
items.explain: Low-latency, offline-resilient requirements favor edge-based processing at a local gateway, with periodic cloud sync for storage/analytics — a hybrid leaning edge, mirroring the Unit 1 edge/fog/cloud trade-off.

items.q: AWS IoT Core securely connects devices using which protocols?
items.explain: AWS IoT Core handles device connectivity over MQTT, HTTP, and WebSockets. Greengrass adds edge compute; SageMaker adds ML; QuickSight adds visualization.

items.q: Confidentiality must be protected in which states of data?
options: Data at rest, data in use, and data in motion
items.explain: Confidentiality of content must hold whether data is stored (at rest), being processed (in use), or transmitted (in motion). Encryption is the primary tool across all three.

items.q: Match the security goal to its primary protection tool: integrity is primarily protected by ___.
items.explain: Integrity (detecting/preventing unauthorized modification) is primarily protected by hash algorithms. Encryption protects confidentiality; digital signatures provide non-repudiation.

items.q: How does a Denial-of-Sleep attack exploit IoT's own design philosophy?
options: Low-power IoT depends on devices sleeping to save battery; denying sleep drains their batteries flat, killing a long deployment without crashing the network
items.explain: IoT's low-power model relies on devices sleeping most of the time. A DoSA keeps them awake (e.g., a fake node forcing constant transmission), draining batteries and making devices unavailable — a DoS on the power budget.

items.q: An attacker obtains a home Wi-Fi password because a device's companion smartphone app stored it insecurely. This is which vulnerability category?
items.explain: Insecure mobile connection: setup apps request Wi-Fi credentials and, if stored insecurely, let attackers who access that storage authenticate as legitimate users and enter the IoT system.

options: The complexity, skill set, and time needed to launch the attack
How easy the threat is to discover
items.explain: Exploitability captures the difficulty (complexity, skills, time) of launching the attack. Damage = how catastrophic; Affected users = scope; Discoverability = how easily found; Reproducibility = how repeatable.

items.q: In the smart EV charging-station example, which were identified as the highest-value data assets?
options: The ground sensor's vacancy bit only
Payment data, license-plate data, and raw video footage
items.explain: The threat model flagged payment data, license-plate data, and raw IP-camera video as the highest-value assets — the most attractive targets requiring the strongest protection.

items.q: Why can 'de-identified' data still be a privacy risk?
options: It can be re-identified when combined with other datasets — true de-identification means NO possibility of identifying an individual
It is the same as personal data by law
items.explain: Removing obvious identifiers isn't enough; integrating de-identified data with other sources can re-identify a person. Legally, data is de-identified only when there is no possibility of identifying an individual.

items.q: The 2015 Jeep hack and 2017 St. Jude cardiac-device findings share which lesson?
options: IoT security failures are only financial
Integrity/availability failures in IoT can be life-threatening (steering a car off the road; wrong cardiac pacing/shocks)
items.explain: Both showed that compromising IoT integrity/availability has physical, life-or-death stakes — controlling a vehicle or a pacemaker — underscoring that IoT security is a safety issue, not just data protection.

items.q: A vaccine cold-chain wants tamper-proof, sensor-by-sensor provenance across many handlers. Why is blockchain a good fit, and what's the catch?
options: Fit: immutable, decentralized, auditable provenance with no single point of failure; Catch: constrained IoT devices struggle with blockchain's compute/storage/energy and low throughput
Fit: it speeds up sensors; Catch: it needs no nodes
Fit: it eliminates sensors; Catch: it is illegal
items.explain: Blockchain gives an immutable, decentralized, auditable record ideal for multi-party provenance. The catch is the tension with constrained, low-power IoT devices and blockchain's heavy compute/storage/energy and limited throughput — addressed with lightweight ledgers and gateway/cloud offload.
